info.bio: Jeffrey Scott Buckley (17 de noviembre de 1966 - 29 de mayo de 1997) fue un cantautor y guitarrista estadounidense. Conocido por su peculiar voz de al menos cuatro octavas y media, los críticos consideraron a Buckley como uno de los artistas más prometedores de su generación tras la publicación en 1994 de su álbum debut "Grace". Sin embargo, en la cumbre de su popularidad, Buckley murió ahogado mientras nadaba en el río Wolfe, en Memphis, TN.

scenes.name: Cantautores lo-fi de los noventa
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: Los noventa son la década del cantautor: la tecnología y las redes informales del post-punk favorecen la carrera en solitario, con Joni Mitchell y Leonard Cohen (no Dylan ni Springsteen) como maestros. El folk sombrío inaugurado por Chris Isaak, Smog y American Music Club se convierte casi en un género: Vic Chesnutt, Mark Lanegan, Mountain Goats, Elliott Smith, Jeff Buckley, Ron Sexsmith, Mike Johnson, Simon Joyner, Songs:Ohia. El neo-pop de Stephen Merritt (Magnetic Fields: Holiday, The Charm Of The Highway Strip, 69 Love Songs), Chris Connelly, Frank Black, Mike Gira (Body Lovers, Angels Of Light), Richard Davies y Eric Matthews (Cardinal), David Gray. El neo-folk de Beck (folk para la era del hip hop), John Frusciante, Sparklehorse, Bright Eyes, Rufus Wainwright, Grandaddy, Bobby Conn; el neo-country de Richard Buckner y Freedy Johnston; Steve Wynn, Mike Watt, Paul Westerberg, Ben Harper.

podcast.title: Accidental Death in 1997
podcast.body: Jeff Buckley tragically died accidentally in 1997 by drowning. The transcript explicitly states that discussing controversies or speculations surrounding his death is "ridículo e innecesario" (ridiculous and unnecessary), emphasizing that the precise circumstances (e.g., suicide) are not relevant, only the unfortunate fact of his accidental passing. "desgraciadamente 1997 no sejaba accidentalmente no voy a entrar en todas las polémicas que hay sobre la morda de jet backly me parece ridículo innecesario el hombre murió agado."

podcast.title: Early Career as a Cover Artist
podcast.body: Jeff Buckley did not begin his career primarily as a singer of his own compositions, but rather as a highly skilled cover artist. He started by performing and reinterpreting numerous songs by other artists. This background, combined with his diverse influences including soul, blues, and classical singer-songwriters like Bob Dylan and Leonard Cohen, made it challenging for him to establish a clear artistic identity initially. "curiosamente al principio no tanto empezo como cantantes y no empezó haciendo versiones de muchos otros temas de mucha gente."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Early Influences and Musical Development
podcast.body: Jeff Buckley, born to Tim Buckley and Mary Guibert, met his father only once. His mother was a classically trained musician, while his stepfather introduced him to bands like Pink Floyd, Jimi Hendrix, The Who, Led Zeppelin, and Queen. Jeff picked up the guitar at age 5, discovered Rush, Kiss, and various prog rock bands, and received his first electric guitar at age 12. "One of the people Tim left behind was his eight-year-old son, Jeff, who admitted his father only once. Mom was a classically trained musician playing piano and cello. Meanwhile, Jeff's death father was into Pink Floyd, Jimmy Hendrix, the who led Zeppelin and Queen. He picked up a guitar at age 5, discovered rush and kiss and various prog rock bands, which led to his first electric guitar at age 12."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Inspiration for "Fake Plastic Trees"
podcast.body: Legend suggests that Tom York's vocal performance on Radiohead's song "Fake Plastic Trees" was directly inspired by the late Jeff Buckley. Radiohead had reportedly seen Buckley perform at a local bar the night before recording the track. "legend has it that Tom's vocal performance on that track was inspired by the late Jeff Buckley, who in the band had seen at a local bar the night before."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Inspiration for Fake Plastic Trees
podcast.body: A Jeff Buckley concert in Oxford directly inspired Radiohead's "Fake Plastic Trees" stylistically. Thom Yorke attended this concert while experiencing a creative block, seeking to develop the idea for the song, and it ultimately became a key influence on its sound. "Es inspirar en Jeff Paky un concierto de Jeff Paky en Noffford, después de que la banda, sobre todo, Antonio Orcubi se entró en una especie de comatascamiento creativo para poder desarrollar bien la idea que tenía de la canción y grabar la fona pesadilla."

podcast.title: Managerial Support
podcast.body: Initial interest in Jeff Buckley's career was sparked after he performed at a memorial concert held in honor of his father, Tim Buckley. During this event, where he reinterpreted his father's songs, he began to generate significant attention. Coincidentally, the first person to show interest in him was his father's former manager, who subsequently helped him secure a "bastante bueno" (quite good) contract with Columbia Records, leading to the recording of his debut album, "Grace." "el primero que se interesó por él curiosamente fue el que había sido el manayer de su padre que fue el que lo ayudó a hacer despegar su carrera."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Path to Recording Deal
podcast.body: As he got older, Jeff Buckley supported himself by working in a hotel while playing gigs. In 1990, his father's former manager helped him create a demo tape, which was circulated to record labels. After some initial setbacks, he performed as a solo artist in New York, where he was discovered and signed to Columbia Records. "When he got older, he started playing gigs while supporting himself working in a hotel. In 1990, his father's former manager helped make him a demo that was shopped around various record labels, and after a couple of dead-ends, he ended up performing as a solo artist in and around New York. He was discovered by Columbia Records, signed a nice deal, and set to work on a demo."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Posthumous Acclaim of "Grace"
podcast.body: Jeff Buckley's sole proper studio album, *Grace*, released in 1994, has become recognized as a classic since his untimely death. "Since then, that one and only proper studio album has become something of a classic."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Posthumous Recognition and Influence
podcast.body: Despite receiving considerable critical recognition from influential figures such as Lou Reed, Patti Smith, Nick Cave, and Bob Dylan during his lifetime, Jeff Buckley did not achieve the widespread public recognition he deserved until after his death in 1997. Over the years, his unique and intimate singing style gained immense respect and became a significant influence for a new generation of artists, including Thom Yorke, the singer of Muse, Rufus Wainwright, and Anthony and the Johnsons, especially as the grunge era waned and more introspective music gained prominence. "con los años a Jeff Buckley se tocá tebra porque la forma de cantar de Jeff Buckley sería una parte sólida muy importante para otros grandes cantantes."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Struggles with Columbia Records
podcast.body: Although Jeff Buckley secured a good contract with Columbia Records, the label did not fully commit to promoting him heavily after the release of "Grace." They did not perceive the album as a huge commercial success nor did they see a clear stylistic direction for his future, which led them to not "apostar demasiado" (bet too much) on him. This limited support, coupled with his modest concert attendance, meant he was continuously forced to perform in small venues to make a living. "Colombia no termina de ver un gran éxito en él tampoco veía un estilo en el que dice demasiado futuro entonces como que tampoco apostó demasiado."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Stylistic Evolution During Second Album Production
podcast.body: During the period he was working on his second album, Jeff Buckley was still in the process of defining his style, which sometimes proved challenging. He was "medio camino entre Nueva York, en Menfis" (halfway between New York, in Memphis), indicating a period of artistic searching and geographic movement as he tried to refine his sound. "en baclí seguía definiendo su estilo lo cual a veces le costaba un poco estaba medio camino entregaba en Nueva York, en Menfis."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Tragic Accidental Drowning
podcast.body: On the evening of May 29, 1997, while in Memphis to record new material, Jeff Buckley went for a swim in Wolf River Harbor, which connects to the Mississippi River. He had swum there before, but this time he entered the water fully clothed and wearing heavy boots. While floating on his back and singing the chorus to Led Zeppelin's "Whole Lotta Love," a boat passed by, creating a wake that caused him to disappear. His body was found five days later downstream. The death was ruled an accidental drowning, with no drugs or alcohol involved and no indication of suicide. He was 30 years old. "Everything was going absolutely according to plan until the evening of May 29, 1997. Jeff was in Memphis to record some new material, and that night he and Keith Fulti, a rodean is banned, sat on the bank of Wolf River Harbor, which is connected to the Mississippi River, listening to music. Jeff had gone swimming there a few times before, and decided to do it again. So he went into the water. This time he was fully clothed and wearing big, heavy boots. He floated out on his back and began seeing the chorus to Led Zeppelin's whole lot of love. But then a boat came by, stirring up a big wake, and with that, Jeff was gone. His body was found five days later down River. No drugs, no alcohol, nothing to indicate suicide. It was a straight, accidental drowning. He was 30 years old."

xref.title: Tom Verlaine Death (January 28, 2023) – Prostate Cancer, Age 73; Helped CBGB Become Ground Zero for Punk
xref.body: Tom Verlaine co-founded Television and in 1973 helped Hilly Kristal — owner of a scuzzy bar on Bleecker Street in a then-terrible part of New York — to let Television play a Sunday night residency. This decision catalyzed CBGB into becoming ground zero for New York punk and, by chain reaction, the entire international punk movement. Television produced two critically acclaimed albums before breaking up in 1978. Verlaine subsequently collaborated with Patti Smith, worked with James Iha of the Smashing Pumpkins, had a song covered by David Bowie, and was involved in a 1992 Television reunion album. He was scheduled to produce Jeff Buckley's second album — a project ended when Buckley drowned in the Mississippi River in 1997. Verlaine was diagnosed with prostate cancer at some point in the 2000s; it metastasized. He died January 28, 2023, age 73. "That was the catalyst for making CBGB ground zero for the world of New York punk."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
